seriesTitle: The Reckoner of the Thirteenth Hour
title: Chapter 8: The Sum Tran Hid
blurb: Tran has been lying about how much sleep he owes, and Petra has two nights to get him under the bench line before the last matchday.

blocks.text: Tran woke thirty-eight minutes after he went under. He was lying on the landing boards beside plate XII with Drewe's coat folded under his head, and the Hour had been over for eighteen of those minutes.
He sat up too fast and put one hand flat on the floor. He looked at Marguerite, then at Drewe, then at me.
'Mm,' he said. 'Rested.'
Nobody laughed. Marguerite took her hand off his sleeve, where it had been since we laid him down.
I had already done the sum.
'You owe about thirty-one hours of sleep, Tran,' I said. 'The Doze Rule benches you over twenty-four, and if you're benched we can't field four.'
He looked at his hands and did not argue.

We had got him off the plate in well under a minute. Marguerite stopped trying to wake him and got behind him instead. She put her arms under his and walked backwards to the rim of XII at half speed, with his heels dragging, and Drewe took his legs on the dead floor. When his second boot left the plate his Still went with it, and XII ran at its own rate again. I wrote the time on my sheet. A held Still runs on its Stiller's clock whether he is awake or not.
I had watched their hands all the way. Marguerite's were white at the knuckles in his coat. Drewe's moved slowly, the way they move on a movement she does not want to drop.
There had been twenty minutes of the Hour left. He slept through all of them. The Regulator struck, we stood on the landing at midnight like anyone else, and he slept on.

When Drewe folded his coat a set of chits came out of the inside pocket, pinned at the corner. They were from the chicory stall at the foot of the tower, one chit a week. Marguerite held them out to me. I took them.

They went back to the week he came to the Ninth Stair from Millrace. Every one said seven stone jugs. Black chicory pays none of the sleep a Stiller owes. It only holds off the sudden sleeps that come once the debt is two days old, and nobody drinks seven jugs a week to hold off sleeps he is not owed.

I had my copies of the Arbiter's sleep ledger from the MD8, MD9 and MD10 checks. At each of them Tran had written eighteen hours. My sheets gave him thirteen minutes of Still since the MD8 check, tonight included, and every minute is an hour owed. His week, as he had given it to me, had no extra sleep in it, and the chits said he had paid none. If the first eighteen was true, he owed thirty-one. I could not know that it was true, so I said 'about'.
'Eighteen,' I said now. 'Three times.'
Tran turned his hands over and looked at the palms. 'Thirty-one and a half before I went down,' he said. 'Thirty-one now.'
Marguerite let out a breath. Drewe's screwdriver stopped turning in her fingers.
'If I write that at the check, there's no match,' Tran said. He said it slowly, the way he says everything. 'Three of you. Forfeit. Twelfth. Gone. I was keeping it off you.'

'You fell asleep on your plate with your Still held and none of us could wake you,' I said. 'If that happens in a match, we lose the round, and you owe an hour for every minute you stand there asleep. If it happens on a tram line, we lose you.'
'Mm.'
'You were hiding a cost from the team. That is a cost to the team. We pay it whether we know about it or not. I would rather know.'
He looked at me then. 'You'd have me write thirty-one.'
'I'd have you write what you owe on the night, whatever it is. If it's over twenty-four, we forfeit, and we go down honestly.'
Drewe tapped the empty chicory jug with her screwdriver. 'Or we let him run down before the check,' she said. 'Properly. No escapement on him.'
Tran held his hand out for my pencil. I gave it to him. He wrote 31 on the back of my training sheet, and when he had written it he looked at it.
I knew what three false lines in an Arbiter's ledger could cost him if anyone ever asked. I did not say it. I put the chits in my coat.
MD11 was two nights off. To pass the check Tran had to pay seven of his thirty-one hours in about forty-four hours, on top of his ordinary sleep.

I wrote his budget at the night desk on graph paper, the way I had written everyone's week. His ordinary night was seven hours. No chicory from that moment. The sudden sleeps would come, and each one would pay what it lasted, so they went on the sheet as payment, provided someone was beside him when they came. Then two long nights: in bed by one and up at noon, then in bed by nine and up at seven. That came to seven and a half hours if the sudden sleeps gave half an hour between them.

Marguerite took his early shift. His gaffer took her on for two days because she was at the gate at six and he was short. She had had no bench to go to since her foreman let her go. Drewe walked Tran wherever he had to be. He slept on Marguerite's floor, the other way round from the week of her Wardle paper, and I sat with him in the mornings, because I do not sleep much and someone had to be awake.
Drewe poured the last jug down the drain on the landing. 'There,' she said. 'Escapement's out. Now he can run down at his own rate.'
Marguerite bet on every hour. She wrote the bets on the back of a pie-shop bill: a copper an hour that he would beat my sheet, hour by hour, and Drewe took the other side of every one.
The first night he slept from one until twenty to twelve. That was three hours and forty minutes over his ordinary night. Marguerite read it off the bill and held her hand out to Drewe.

The next day he went under twice. The first time was at the Guild Hall stop. Drewe caught him by the coat, sat him on the bench, and he slept twenty-five minutes with his head on her shoulder while two trams came and went. The second time was on Marguerite's stair. He sat down on the fourth step and was gone, and she sat on the third and held his ankle for half an hour so he could not slide.
The second night he was in bed at nine and woke at five to seven. That was two hours and fifty-five minutes over.
I added it on the sheet at the desk. Seven hours and thirty minutes paid. He owed twenty-three and a half.
Marguerite had won three coppers off Drewe and lost five. She paid up on the landing, one coin at a time, and called each one by the hour it had lost on.

The Arbiter set up her table at the head of the stair at half past eleven on MD11 night. Tran filled in his line in the sleep ledger with me beside him. He wrote 'twenty-three and a half'. He looked at the page while he wrote it, and he looked at it after. The Arbiter read it, said 'At or below,' and blotted it.

We were eleventh on eleven points. A win would lift us to tenth and safety. A loss would put us twelfth and out of the League. A draw would leave us eleventh, in the Daylight Playoff against the Queue champion.

Ropewalk came up the stair at a quarter to twelve, a full five behind Askew. The two Sprinters were young and quick on the steps and bright in the eyes. They looked at our plates as if they could not wait to stand on them. Three more Ropewalk players came up behind and sat on the far bench in their coats.
At the League office Askew had told me her Sprinters came to her grey.

I sat down beside Marguerite on our bench and told her, and no one else. 'My silence answered her,' I said. 'She's booking their stalls into their sleep, the way we do.' I looked at the far bench. 'And she's brought the rest of her roster to watch how we play four.'
Marguerite looked across at the two Sprinters. She did not bet.
'I'm afraid we've lost the one edge we had,' I said.
'Then we play without it,' Marguerite said. 'Like everybody else.'
Drewe had Mabry's box in her coat on the bench hook. She would wind nothing from it, as we had agreed.

Ropewalk's Sprinters spent every second Askew issued them, in every round. Askew banked four in the first Bank minute. She banked four in the second, and four in every one after it, whether Ropewalk were ahead or behind.

In the fourth round and again in the eighth, a Ropewalk Sprinter came on to XII straight at the side Tran was facing. I was frozen both times, as I am in every Lull. I put the runs together afterwards. The Tally showed twenty-two spent by Ropewalk in the fourth and nineteen in the eighth. The Arbiter ruled a Spill on XII both times. The Token lay dead where Tran's touch had set it down, and both rounds ran out with nobody scoring. Tran's Still had sprung for both, so he had seen them.
'She came at my face,' he said after the eighth. 'Walked into my hand. Mm.'
My verdict was that Askew had not been trying to score with those two runs. She was finding out how fast Tran turned and whether he was awake, and she had found out that he was.

After eleven rounds of play Ropewalk had ten points and we had nine. They had scored three runs and we had scored two. The banks had gone five to us and four to them, with one tied. The Tally showed us two hundred and thirty-four spent and twenty-nine banked, and Ropewalk two hundred and thirty-eight spent and forty banked. That left thirty-seven in our jar to bid or issue, and twenty-two in theirs.
The jars closed for the eleventh Bank minute. Tran came to the inner rim of XII, the nearest point of his plate to the Arbor. Ropewalk had nobody on XII in that minute.
'I'm going under,' he said, low. 'Not yet. Close. I can keep it Set. I can't hold a full sprung Still. If she comes at me with a long spend in the twelfth, I'll go down in the middle of it.'
I watched his hands. His thumbs were pressed hard into the sides of his first fingers, the way a man pinches himself to stay awake. They did not let go while he spoke.

My plan had needed him. If I banked five and Askew banked her four, we won the point and drew level, with thirty-two in our jar against her eighteen. Then she could not win the last bank. She would have to come at XII in the twelfth with everything she had. Tran would Spill her, she would come out of it with less than us, and we would win the bank, the match and tenth place.
The plan needed a Keep who could hold a full sprung Still.

There was a run. The Token starts the twelfth on XII, under Tran's boots. The only run from there began with Tran lifting it with no Still and stepping off on to the dead floor, so that Marguerite could lift it from XI. Then it was six plates to VI through two Ropewalk Stillers, with no Keep on XII for as long as it took. My sheets said a run like that cost forty seconds at the least. We had thirty-seven. An issue of forty would be an Overdraw: nothing issued, Marguerite frozen for the rest of the round, and a penalty point to Ropewalk. An issue of thirty-seven would run short, with nothing left in the jar to bank. Either way we lost.

So there was the bank. If I banked nineteen and Askew banked four, we won the point, and each jar held eighteen. With the jars level she could not win the last bank, and she could not lose it unless she spent. She could come at Tran with all eighteen and win the match, or sit and draw it. She would have to choose without knowing what he had just told me.
'Bao,' I said. 'I believe you. Keep it Set and stay on your feet.'
It was the first time I had said his name. He nodded once and walked back to the centre of the plate.
I wrote nineteen on the slate. The Arbiter turned both slates together. Askew's said four. Mine said nineteen.
Ten each. Eighteen in each jar. We went into the twelfth level.

I issued nobody. Askew issued nobody. For four minutes the landing was live play and nothing else. Ropewalk's quicker Sprinter stood on I, one stride from XII, beside Marguerite, and watched Tran. Drewe stood on XI.
I watched Tran's hands. They hung at his sides. Twice the right one closed and opened. Once his chin went down, and Drewe said 'Bao,' not loudly, and it came up again.
The Ropewalk Sprinter did not move. The round ended with the Token where it had started, under Tran's boots.

Then the last Bank minute. Askew had banked four in eleven Bank minutes. I wrote eighteen, which was everything we had and which could not lose. I held the slate face down on the Arbor rail until the Arbiter asked for it.
She turned them together. Askew's said eighteen.
Equal banks score nothing. Ten each, a draw. Twelve points. Eleventh. The Daylight Playoff.
Bao sat down on his plate where he stood, put his head on his knees, and was asleep before the Arbiter had blotted the score.

The Close was in the porter's lodge at the foot of our tower, with the spot-check clerk. I checked the scale read zero on the empty pan. Issue three hundred, spent two hundred and thirty-four, so the jar should hold sixty-six. It read sixty-six. It was cold in my bare hands. Variance column: MD11, none, cold.

Marguerite's two hundred and thirty-four minutes went into her three o'clocks, as before, and she said yes to every line. There was nothing to book for Drewe. Bao's Still time on my sheet came to three minutes and fifty-one seconds. On top of his twenty-three and a half, he now owed a little over twenty-seven hours, and three hours and fifty-one minutes of it fell due inside two days. I wrote it on a fresh sheet and gave it to him when he woke. He read it all the way down.
'Mm,' he said.
Askew was waiting on the turn of the stair below the lodge, pulling her gloves on.
'I'll tell you what I did,' she said, 'since you won't ask.'
I said nothing. She did not wait for me to.

'Ropewalk hold eight on the roster. Tonight I lodged two reserves as my Sprinters. Neither of them had spent a second all Turn. They owe nothing. My regulars sat on the bench in their coats.' She buttoned the second glove. 'Fresh legs. Not practised ones. A practised Sprinter doesn't run at a Keep's face, and mine did it twice.'
The three on the far bench had been her grey ones. I had told Marguerite she brought them to watch us.
'And the twelfth?' I said.

'Your jar was level with mine. I wasn't sending two children who'd never spent before tonight at a Keep who'd held all night, for the lot.' She looked at me the way she had at the League office counter. 'I still don't know how your lot play four and come up fresh. I will by next Turn.'
'I thought you'd copied us,' I said. 'I was wrong about you.'
She nodded as if she had expected that much and no more. I did not tell her what she would have found. She went on down the stair.
Marguerite had waited at the top, by the stair door. She had not made a bet since the Close. When I reached her she did not move to go down.
'Somebody's seen Felix,' she said. 'Wardle. Two of the old Copper lot saw him on a landing last week, with a jar under his arm.'
She said it very quietly. Her hands were in her coat pockets, and they stayed there all the way down the stair. She said nothing else.
The League posted the Daylight Playoff the next afternoon, on the board over the east gate. The Ninth Stair, eleventh in the Stairwell League, would play the champion of the Queue for our place.
The Queue champion was the Sleepless Hands, sponsored by Dunstan Mabry and Reckoned by Felix Wardle.
